open_obligations: Check that the toy-setting remark applies to Khan et al. [13] and not only to Radhakrishnan [23], which is grouped with it and is not in the atlas
Do not extend the toy-setting remark to Irving et al. [12], which is cited in the same group but does not use QuALITY
Check that the 'judges have not read' description matches Khan et al.'s hidden-passage protocol

out.other_title: Expertise gap is only information access; RLHF debaters have an honesty propensity
out.rationale: McAleese et al. say previous work [12, 13, 23] has demonstrated that oversight methods like debate have the potential to help humans more accurately assess the answers to reading comprehension questions, and their reference list gives [13] as Khan et al., Debating with more persuasive LLMs leads to more truthful answers (2402.06782). They note these works apply their methods primarily to multiple choice questions about short science fiction stories that the judges have not read, and say that toy setting was invaluable for early scalable oversight. Khan et al. state as a limitation that in their setup the difference between strong and weak is only in access to information. The remark bears on that limitation, since it calls the setting of works including Khan et al., where the judges have not read the stories, a toy setting. The cited lines stop before saying what the toy setting lacks and do not argue that the difference is only in access to information, so the remark is not an argument for Khan et al.'s limitation and the link proposes only ADDRESSES.
out.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: Limits of results for oversight methods like debate obtained on multiple choice questions about short science fiction stories that the judges have not read
